lede: Naga (sacred serpent) accounts for 9 catalogued manuscripts. It clusters in Mae Hong Son (33% of the corpus for this subject), ahead of Lamphun and Lampang. Nearly all (89%) are written in Tham Lanna · อักษรธรรมล้านนา script. By support it leans to palm-leaf · ใบลาน (78%) over khoi paper · กระดาษข่อย (11%). Dated witnesses run 1713–1974 CE (9 of 9 carry a date).

authored.title: Naga (sacred serpent)
authored.body_html:
What this is

The naga (นาค; Pali nāga) is the water-serpent of Southeast Asian cosmology — lord of the rivers and of the treasure under the ground, storm-bringer and rain-giver, and in the Buddhist frame a being of enormous power who chose to kneel. In the Lanna world he is not one thing. He is a character in a birth-tale, a shape you draw with a particular opening syllable, a candle you roll to cancel a bad year, an alloy you beat into a takrut, a name your family calls you on the morning you ordain, and a stone balustrade you put your hand on climbing to a shrine. This page follows him through all of those — the story first, then the witnesses, then the working naga in the printed manuals, where he turns out to be far busier than a title search suggests.

The story, first

Tradition holds — the founding image is the naga who did not strike. In the weeks after the awakening, a storm comes down on the Buddha sitting under a mucalinda tree, and the serpent-king Mucalinda rises out of the roots, winds his coils seven times around the seated body and spreads his hood over the head like a roof, holding the rain off for seven days. Then, the story says, he unwinds, takes the form of a young man, and stands before the Buddha with his hands together. Everything else the naga does in this tradition is a footnote to that gesture: enormous force, voluntarily bent to shelter. It is why the coiled serpent with the fanned hood is carved behind Buddha images, why he runs down every temple stair-rail with the whole flight of steps disappearing into his mouth, and why he rears up as the ช่อฟ้า finial at the roof-ridge — the building itself held in a serpent's grip, protectively.

Tradition holds — the second story is why a Thai man is called a naga on the day he ordains. In the Vinaya's telling, a naga so admired the monastic life that he took human shape and got himself ordained; asleep in his hut, he relaxed back into his true body, and a monk who came to wake him found the room full of serpent. The Buddha sent him away — an animal cannot hold the training — and the naga wept and asked that his name at least be kept. It was. Every candidate for ordination in Thailand is still called นาค. He is shaved as a naga, dressed in white as a naga, carried around the ordination hall as a naga, and only stops being one at the moment the robes go on. The most ordinary rite in the Thai calendar is built on a serpent's disappointment.

Tradition holds — the third naga is the working one. He governs water, so he governs the year: the old almanacs open with a count of how many nagas will "give water" — one naga means a heavy year, seven or eight means a thin one, and the reckoning inverts the way a westerner expects, because the more of them share the labour the less each one pours. He sleeps beneath the ground in a slow annual circuit, and his head-and-tail alignment tells a builder which way to cut the first post, a gravedigger which way to lay the body, and a householder which direction not to dig this season — get it backwards and you have driven a spade into the serpent's face. On the Mekong he is พญานาค Phaya Nak, whose fireballs rise off the river at the end of the Rains Retreat, and whose household on the Thai side has taken names and personalities — Pu Si Sutho and Ya Si Pathum of the Kham Chanot grove chief among them. That last register is modern, popular, and booming, and it shows up in this archive's market data below.

Inference — hold those three together and the shape of the evidence stops being surprising. The naga of story sits in the jātaka shelf under his own name. The naga of wichaa does not get titles, because he is never the subject of a manual — he is an ingredient inside one. So a title search finds the first and misses the second almost entirely, and the printed treatises are where the second one is waiting.

The witnesses that carry his name

Nine manuscripts in the catalogue put a naga in the title. They fall into four small clusters; eight of the nine are in Tham Lanna, and seven are on palm leaf.

  • มหานาควัตถุ Mahanak watthu, "the Matter of the Great Naga" — three copies, all from Wat Kittiwong in Mae Sariang district, Mae Hong Son: ms 1271 (1713, 9 folios, "slightly damaged," dated in the colophon by the year-name pi ka sai), ms 1283 (1722), and ms 1270 (1733), this last one catalogued as Untitled with the title supplied in brackets. The source classes all three as นิยายธรรม, "Buddhist tale." And they are probably not about a serpent at all. Each carries a second, older PLMP cataloguing title underneath the modern one, and the three disagree: ms 1270 says มหานาควัตถุ, agreeing; ms 1283 says มหานาคเถรวัตถุ, "the Matter of the Elder Mahānāga"; and ms 1271 says มหาพกุลเถรวัตถุ, the story of the elder Mahābakkula, a different monk entirely. Inference — Mahānāga is an ordinary Pali monastic name — the same joke the ordination hall plays, one register up — and two of the three cards read this as a monk's life. The archive's largest apparent naga cluster is its least certain, and reading nine folios would settle it. Until someone does, count these three softly.
  • ปุณณะนาคกุมมาน / สุปุณณะนาค Punnanak kumman and Supunnanak — four witnesses of what looks like one work and its variant: ms 3305 (1881) and ms 3306 (1910), both without recorded provenance; ms 3307 at Wat Ban Caem, Lamphun (1969); and ms 4285 (1974). All four are filed as jātaka, and the late dates are notable — this serpent tale was still being copied out by hand in Lanna in the 1970s.
  • นาคเขาคำ Nak khao kham — the title reads as "the naga of Khao Kham," the golden hill — ms 3243, from Wat Pa O Don Chai in Mueang district, Chiang Rai, dated 1970: 14 fascicles, 16 folios, complete, with a colophon, in Pali and Thai, in Thai script on khoi paper. Both of those last facts make it an outlier — it is one of only 56 khoi manuscripts in the whole collection, and one of only 72 in plain Thai script against 6,266 in Tham Lanna. Inference — a naga tale copied late, in the everyday script, on the everyday paper, is a naga tale that had left the scriptorium and gone into circulation.
  • นาควิมานสูตร Nakawimana sut — ms 4835, bound with the Pathainya sut, at Wat Phra That Lampang Luang, Lampang, dated 1787 by the year-name pi moeng mot; 15 folios, filed under Buddhist canonical as a sutta. This is the single non-narrative naga title in the collection — a vimāna text, an account of a celestial mansion and the deeds that earned it, which is to say a naga treated as a destination rather than a character.

Inference — subtract the Wat Kittiwong cluster and the catalogue's title-level naga shrinks to six, which sharpens rather than weakens what follows: the serpent who is genuinely well attested on this shelf is not called naga in a title at all. He is called Bhūridatta.

Bhūridatta — the serpent who took the precepts

The old version of this page named "the Bhūridatta-type serpent-king tales" and left it there. The catalogue has them, and they are not a footnote: eighteen witnesses carry ภูริทัต / Phulitat in the title, all palm-leaf, all Tham Lanna, all filed as jātaka, with dated copies running 1722 to 1955. They cluster in Lampang (7) and Chiang Mai (6) — three at Wat Duang Di alone (1789, 1825, 1844), two at Wat Chedi Luang, and single copies as far out as Wat Phra That Hariphunchai in Lamphun. Bhūridatta is twice as well attested in this archive as every manuscript that names a naga in its title — and three times better attested than the ones that securely do.

Tradition holds — the story is the reason. Bhūridatta is a naga prince who takes the eight precepts and, to keep them, coils himself on an anthill at the edge of the human world and vows not to move — not to defend himself — for the whole night, offering his skin, flesh and blood to anyone who wants them. A snake-charmer takes him at his word: catches him with charms, crushes him in his hands, breaks his bones, stuffs him into a basket and makes him dance in village after village for money. He does not resist, because resisting would break the vow, and the vow is the only thing he came for. The corpus's own devotional mnemonics compress the whole thing into a phrase — in the Great Assembly invocation printed in the Compendium of Ancient Katha he is listed among the Ten Births as "Phra Bhuridatta, who observed the precepts and gave alms." Inference — that is why he out-copies the rest. The Lanna shelf does not want the naga as a monster; it wants the naga as the being with the most to lose by being good, and losing it.

The working naga — nine jobs in the printed treatises

The contributed printed manuals are where the second naga lives, and he is everywhere in them. He is almost never the topic of a page. He is a shape, a syllable, a metal, a witness, a candle.

He is a shape with its own password. The charm-and-amulet treatise (p.14) gives the inscription formulas keyed to what you are drawing. A banner-shaped yant opens ธะชัคคังปะริตตัง มังคะลัง. A lotus-petal yant opens ปะทุมะยันตัง สันตัง วิกรึงคะเร. And a naga-shaped yant opens นาคะยันตัง สันตัง วิกรึงคะเร — the same ground-formula with the serpent's name slotted in where the shape's name goes. The naga is a declension of the general yantra grammar, not a special case.

He is a candle you burn down to the end of your bad luck. The Lanna yantra-and-katha manual gives the full procedure for วิชายันต์เทียนพญานาคสะเดาะเคราะห์, the Naga-King Candle-Yantra for Dispelling Misfortune, and the procedure is the article. First write the person out in full — given name, surname, day, month, BE year, year of birth, age. Then name the yantra aloud, in the formula, so that the thing knows what it is: "this candle-yantra should accordingly be called the Naga-King Candle-Yantra for Dispelling Misfortune." Then wake it with a Pali awakening-verse. Then build it: take one strand of sacred thread longer than the person's age, roll it for a wick, lay a sheet of beeswax in the sun until it is "moderately softened — judge this by feel," and roll the candle with a head and a tail. Then light it before the Buddha image and sit reciting until the candle burns out. The wick is longer than the life it is for, and the rite ends when the wax runs out — the same logic that drives the life-extension rite, told in wax.

He is the thing the diagram stands on. Two pages later the same manual prints a tower of stacked script-panels crowned with a lotus-bud finial, and underneath it a naga, coiled so that his raised head and tail curve up on either side to form a boat-like base beneath the whole figure. Not decoration: the serpent is the hull the yant travels in.

He is a stencil you can take to a tattooist. The sak-yant tracing book carries ยันต์พญานาค twice over — a coiled serpent-dragon with a flame-tipped tail and a spiral amulet-mark at the centre of the coil, ringed by fine cursive incantation script, then a second variant with the head turned toward a burst of radiating marks. Earlier in the same book a five-row นาคราช yant is printed directly beside a five-row Ganesha — a rearing scaled serpent flanked by five vertical columns of script, filed as one entry in a repertoire of powers.

He is a glyph in the na canon. The Scripture of 108 Magical Na (p.93) runs a gallery of little machines of loop, zigzag and coil, each with a name: Na Son Luk (hiding the child), Na Son Chu (hiding the lover), Na Chang (elephant), Na Suea (tiger), Na Ngu (snake) — and then, immediately after the snake, นะนาคราช, the Naga-King Na, an open crescent-hook over a capsule frame. The snake and the serpent-king are adjacent entries and different glyphs; the tradition files them separately on purpose. (The whole gallery is walkable at the 108 Na.)

He is a heart-syllable. The Khom-Thai inscription formulas (p.23) lists the heart — the compressed syllable-core — of each power in the curriculum, and gives อะงะสะ, "the heart of the Naga King," heading a column that runs on down through the Horse King, the Lord of Death, the Mara King and Thao Wessuwan to the heart of the wild junglefowl that the Kai page follows. Whatever else he is, in the syllable canon he is a standard entry, learnable like any other.

He is worn on the body — as an ornament, in the invocation. The Compendium of Ancient Katha carries a teacher-assembling katha that dresses the practitioner in deities, part by part: the Buddha above the crown and hair, Brahma on the left shoulder, Narayana on the right, the River Goddess as saliva, the Wind God as the breath of the mouth — and the naga prince as a necklace. The serpent goes where the serpent goes in every temple carving: around the throat, above the heart.

He is an alloy. In the Phetcharat great yantra manual (p.77) a takrut instruction lists the metals to inscribe on: gold, นาค, silver, copper — nak here being the reddish gold-copper alloy that carries the serpent's name in Thai metallurgy. The naga is not invoked on that page; he is simply one of the four things you can beat thin enough to write on. Readers working the material lens will recognise the move: a mythic name doing quiet duty as a technical term.

And he is leverage in a love-charm. The Akhom of Phra Narai (p.169) runs a page of one-line attraction mantras with their delivery instructions, and among them: "อิสสะราชา นาคะราชา — this mantra is blown toward a woman so that she comes to love us." No explanation, no myth, no apparatus. The serpent-king's name is simply the strongest thing on the shelf, so it goes in the breath.

The assembly — where the corpus counts the nagas

Two treatises in this collection stop and take the roll.

The Mind-Stream Key to Saiyasat (p.129) is working through the Mahāsamaya Sutta, the great gathering in the Mahāvana forest, and reaches "Part 4: Concerning Nagas and Elephants." They arrive by watershed: the nagas of the pool named Nabhasa in the territory of Vesali, with the retinue of Tacchaka Nagaraja; Kambala and Assatara; the nagas of the ford at Payāga with their kinsfolk; the nagas of the Yamuna; the whole Dhataraṭṭha clan with their households. Then the elephant Erāvaṇa. Then — Part 5 — the garudas, "those divine birds who have clear eyes and are able to swoop and seize naga kings suddenly." And here the commentary does something lovely with the fear in the room: "At that time, fearlessness arose for all the nagas, because the Buddha had extended his spiritual power, making them safe from the Garuda king." The gloss goes on to explain the ordinary state of affairs — naga-devas live in water, garuda-devas live in trees and on mountains, they are enemies by nature — "but when they came together at this assembly in the Mahavana forest, they all became friends with one another." An armistice, in a forest, for the length of a sermon. Elsewhere in the corpus the war is back on: the same Compendium (p.52) carries คาถาพญาครุฑ, the Spell of the Garuda King, in which the speaker declares himself the garuda-lord arriving before the Naga King and commands him aside.

The Supreme Maha Mantra Katha takes the roll differently — as blessing. Its long litany works through arahants and nuns and then arrives at the nagas and simply names them, four to a verse, for verse after verse: Sumana, Sumanacala, Aravāḷa, Eḷapattaka, Campeyya, Mucalinda, Kambala; then Kāla, Mahākāla, Saṅkhapāla, Mahodara, Maṇikaṇṭha, Maṇiakkhi, Nanda and Upananda; then Varuṇa, Dhataraṭṭha, Kuṅkuvila, Apalāla, Citra, Mahāvīra, Chabyāputta, Vāsukī; then Kaṇhāgotama, Aggisikha, Cūḷodara, Ahicchatta, "the naga kings, with Erāpatha and the rest as their leaders." And then the ask, which is the best sentence about nagas in the whole archive: "Whatever naga kings there are, of fierce venom — that is, venom that spreads swiftly — of dreadful poison, having their eyes as weapons, dwelling in the water or dwelling on land, dwelling in the mountains, or roaming in the rivers — may all those naga kings grant us excellent well-being, long life, and freedom from illness at all times." Thirty-odd names of the most dangerous beings in the cosmology, recited in order, so that they will look after you.

Inference — this is the naga's real position in the ritual grammar of these books, and it is why he keeps appearing without ever getting a chapter. He is neither worshipped nor exorcised. He is convened. The Vedic katha for chai chatri (p.2) makes it explicit in its deity-convening formula, the one you say before anything else: "and the great naga-kings, standing near — the deities dwell in every islet and rapids of every district" — invited in the same breath as the ruesi and the sky-devas, with the instruction printed plainly underneath: "Before performing any rite whatsoever, one should first recite this Katha for Convening the Deities." Every rite in these manuals begins by telling the serpents in the local water that something is about to happen.

The naga a monk had to fight

One naga in the corpus is not convened but subdued, and he is famous enough to be sung weekly. Verse 7 of the Jaya Maṅgala Gāthā — the Bāhung, printed in the Lanna yantra manual — runs: "The naga king Nandopananda, learned and of great power, was tamed by the elder [Moggallāna], his own disciple, appearing as a naga — through the method of teaching miraculous power the Lord of Sages conquered him." Moggallāna wins by becoming what he is fighting.

That verse turns up again as evidence in an argument. In Teaching Meditation and Psychic Power (p.156) the author is defending the study of mind-power against learned monks who say it is a later accretion, "a low-level branch of knowledge that should not be studied," and he reaches for the Bāhung: eight displays of iddhi in the canon, seven of them by the Buddha himself, and one delegated — "the Buddha taught a stratagem or method for fighting the nāga king to Phra Mahā Moggallāna, then had Moggallāna display iddhi to fight the nāga king." Then, having won the point, he immediately concedes the other half of it: such power exists, "but it is not good, not proper, and is not something befitting the station of the Buddha and the Arahants to do." Inference — a modern Thai author using a serpent-fight to argue that serpent-fighting is real and unbecoming, on the same page, is a fair portrait of how this whole tradition holds its powers.

The naga on the ordination-day list

The plainest naga in the archive is not sacred at all — it is a checklist. The complete ritual handbook, a modern printed manual of ceremonies, sets out the Rite of Going Forth and Higher Ordination, and it uses นาค flatly, as the ordinary word for the man being ordained. The items to prepare (p.18): ผ้านุ่งนาค, cloth for the naga to wear; a raised tray for the triple robe; a ceremonial fan; flowers to drape over the robes; one-baht coins to scatter as alms; and "three lotus flowers, three incense sticks and two candles — for the naga." Then the order of events, which is the naga's last hour: โกนผมนาค, shave the naga's head; แห่นาครอบอุโบสถ, carry the naga in procession around the ordination hall; pay respect to the boundary stones; นาคเข้าสู่อุโบสถ, the naga enters. Inside, he kneels, bows three times, turns to face his parents, bows again, and takes the triple robe from their hands; he walks on his knees to the preceptor; he goes out behind the hall to change; and when he comes back in the robes, the manual has stopped calling him a naga and started calling him a novice. Where two men ordain together the manual has a word for that too — the นาคคู่, the paired nagas (p.32).

The example this handbook prints for the group rite is "a group ordination of naga among Royal Thai Air Force officials," with a chaplain requesting the precepts and a presiding officer working down the order of service. Inference — nothing in this section is mythological, and that is the point. The Vinaya's rejected serpent has ended up as a piece of Thai administrative vocabulary, on a printed schedule, in an air force ceremony. It is the single most thoroughly domesticated naga in the collection.

The living market

The serpent is also the fastest-moving folk figure in the archive's market layer. Of the 13,020 amulet listings in the Lazada snapshot, 79 name พญานาค, นาคราช or พระยานาค in the title — brass takrut, coiled figures, rings, ลูกแก้วพญานาค naga crystal-orbs, and บ่วงนาคบาศ, the naga-noose. Prices sit low and fast: median ฿85, from ฿7 to ฿3,190. The Mekong household is present and named — 5 listings invoke คำชะโนด, the Kham Chanot grove, and 4 name ปู่ศรีสุทโธ, its naga lord. The effect vocabulary is trade and flow: wealth-drawing, เรียกทรัพย์, "money pouring in." Inference — this is the naga register the palm-leaf catalogue is silent about and the printed manuals only glance at, running at full volume in the present tense, and it is Isan-inflected rather than Lanna — the Mekong's serpent, sold nationally. A crawl that treated Phaya Nak as a Lanna subject would miss where his current centre of gravity actually is.

Notes

  • The count to remember is nine, six, and eighteen. Nine manuscripts put นาค in the title; probably only six are about a naga; and eighteen more, on the jātaka shelf, name Bhūridatta, who is one. The old version of this page reported eight and did not count Bhūridatta at all. Any future naga tally should start from the birth-tale hero, not the word.
  • Wat Kittiwong's cluster needs a reader — and this is the correction. The three Mahanak watthu witnesses (ms 1270, 1271, 1283) carry older PLMP titles that read two of them as an elder's life, มหานาคเถรวัตถุ and มหาพกุลเถรวัตถุ, not a serpent's. Nine folios of transcription resolves the archive's biggest naga cluster one way or the other. It is the cheapest high-value job on this page.
  • The functional naga is a section-level phenomenon. Everything in "The working naga" above came from page content, not titles, and all of it from the contributed printed shelf. Inference — the same material is near-certainly sitting inside untitled ยันต์-and-คาถา bundles from Nan, Phrae and Lampang, invisible to a title search. The search image is now specific: look for the opening นาคะยันตัง สันตัง วิกรึงคะเร, for the heart-syllable อะงะสะ, for a candle rite measured against a person's age, and for a coiled base under a yant-tower.
  • Where else he is standing. Read this page beside Mahāsamaya for the assembly, yantra and katha for the forms he is filed under, and Vessantara — the two of them share the same devotional furniture — the great invocation at the Compendium runs through the Ten Births and names Bhūridatta and Vessantara a few names apart, on one breath.
